generatedProse.concept-context: In psychology, a research proposal shapes a study before any data are collected. It names the focused question, often a hypothesis, explains why it is worth testing, and sets out the design: who the participants are, what will be measured, and how. Working through these questions turns a broad interest, say in memory or motivation, into a study you could actually run, with clear limits.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students are interested in the same broad area, memory, and each writes a short proposal.

Tom writes that memory is fascinating and important, lists several things that could be studied, and promises to read widely and report back. The proposal is enthusiastic, but it sets no focused question and no design. With nothing to guide it, the project could go anywhere, and Tom will struggle to know when it is finished.

Amara works through a series of questions: what exactly do I want to find out, what is already known, what fresh angle am I taking, and how will I measure it? Each answer narrows the project to one testable question, with a clear design and limits. The proposal has become a framework.

Both students began with the same interest. Only Amara used guiding questions to shape it into a study that can actually be run.
generatedProse.summary: In psychology, a research proposal shapes a study: it turns a broad interest into a focused, testable question with a design you can carry out. Built from a series of guiding questions, it becomes a framework for the whole project. You can now explain what a proposal is for and recognise how guiding questions do the shaping. The next lesson looks at the shape a study takes on the page.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that turned a broad interest into a workable study?

items.text: She worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one testable question with a clear design.
She promised to read widely and report back on the whole area of memory.
She listed several things about memory that could be studied.
She chose a topic that was more interesting than Tom's.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara used guiding questions to narrow the interest into one testable question with a clear design.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that narrowed the interest and set a design, rather than widening it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara worked through guiding questions that narrowed the interest to one testable question with a clear design. Reading widely or listing possibilities leaves the study unshaped.
